scenes.tts: Why is a cell the size it is? Start with one reason. Everything a cell takes in crosses its surface. Everything it uses is spread through its volume. So what happens as a cell grows?
scenes.visual: A cell with a question mark; blue arrows cross its surface, orange dots fill its volume, then the cell grows.
scenes.narration: Why is a cell the size it is? Start with one reason. Everything a cell takes in crosses its surface. Everything it uses is spread through its volume. So what happens as a cell grows?

scenes.tts: Take a hypothetical smooth spherical cell. Let its radius grow from five micrometres to ten. The area rises fourfold. The volume rises eightfold. Area is four pi r squared. Volume is four pi r cubed over three. For a sphere, the ratio of area to volume is three divided by the radius. So the ratio halves, from zero point six to zero point three per micrometre.
scenes.caption: Take a hypothetical smooth spherical cell. Let its radius grow from 5 micrometres to 10. The area rises fourfold. The volume rises eightfold. Area is 4πr². Volume is 4πr³/3. For a sphere, the ratio of area to volume is 3 divided by the radius. So the ratio halves, from 0.6 to 0.3 per micrometre.
scenes.visual: Cell grows from 5 to 10 micrometres; area bar grows 4 times, volume bar 8 times; the ratio halves.
scenes.narration: Take a hypothetical smooth spherical cell. Let its radius grow from 5 micrometres to 10. The area rises fourfold. The volume rises eightfold. Area is 4πr². Volume is 4πr³/3. scenes.tts: Now invent two rates. They are made-up inputs, not measurements. Say the membrane can take up a nutrient at no more than twenty molecules per square micrometre each second. Say the cell uses six molecules per cubic micrometre each second, evenly through its volume. Assume the whole surface takes up nutrient, and nothing else limits the cell.
scenes.caption: Now invent two rates. They are made-up inputs, not measurements. Say the membrane can take up a nutrient at no more than 20 molecules per square micrometre each second. Say the cell uses 6 molecules per cubic micrometre each second, evenly through its volume. Assume the whole surface takes up nutrient, and nothing else limits the cell.
scenes.visual: Cell with uptake arrows on its whole surface and dots through its volume; two cards give the made-up rates.
scenes.narration: Now invent two rates. They are made-up inputs, not measurements. Say the membrane can take up a nutrient at no more than 20 molecules per square micrometre each second. Say the cell uses 6 molecules per cubic micrometre each second, evenly through its volume. Assume the whole surface takes up nutrient, and nothing else limits the cell.

scenes.tts: Now compare supply with demand. At five micrometres, supply is six thousand two hundred eighty-three molecules per second. Demand is three thousand one hundred forty-two. So supply is twice demand. At ten micrometres, supply only just meets demand. The ratio is exactly one. Supply keeps up to a radius of three times twenty divided by six. That is ten micrometres.
scenes.caption: Now compare supply with demand. At 5 micrometres, supply is 6,283 molecules per second. Demand is 3,142. So supply is twice demand. At 10 micrometres, supply only just meets demand. The ratio is exactly 1. Supply keeps up to a radius of 3 times 20 divided by 6. That is 10 micrometres.
scenes.visual: Supply and demand curves against radius; markers at 5 then 10 micrometres with the readout.
scenes.narration: Now compare supply with demand. At 5 micrometres, supply is 6,283 molecules per second. Demand is 3,142. So supply is twice demand. At 10 micrometres, supply only just meets demand. The ratio is exactly 1. Supply keeps up to a radius of 3 times 20 divided by 6. That is 10 micrometres.

scenes.tts: The arithmetic leaves things out. Change the rates or the shape, and the answer changes. A flat or long thin cell keeps much more surface per volume than a sphere. A plant vacuole can fill most of the cell. A root epidermal cell adds volume mostly as vacuole, so its cytoplasm grows far less than the cell does. In Arabidopsis root epidermis, cells grew about fourteen-fold in volume. The space between vacuole and cell boundary grew only about two to threefold.

scenes.tts: Keep the rule. Supply comes in through the surface. Demand is spread through the volume. As the radius grows, the ratio of capacity to demand falls. In this model it is ten divided by the radius. That is a scaling penalty, not a universal maximum.
